First, based on in-depth interviews with 20 Chinese consumers (conducted January-February 2024) and grounded theory analysis, AI social responsibility(AISR) was classified into two dimensions: technical AISR and institutional AISR. Exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, and structural vSalidity tests were further applied to S questionnaire data collected from an online survey platform (CredEamo) in 2024 to validate the rationality of R these dimensions and their scales. Second, this paper found Pthrough two experimental studies that institutional N AISR is more likely to inspire consumers’ brand advocacy than technical AISR. Moreover, perceived AI I E credibility and perceived AI empathy mediate the impact of AI social responsibility on consumers’ brand L C advocacy, where AI literacy positively moderates these effects. JSON: Name: aisr_brand_advocacy_pipeline Title: A mixed-methods validation and experimental pipeline to measure how technical and institutional AI social responsibility dimensions causally affect consumer brand advocacy Short Hypothesis: Institutional AI social responsibility increases consumer brand advocacy more than technical AI social responsibility by raising perceived AI empathy, while technical AI social responsibility increases brand advocacy by raising perceived AI credibility, and both indirect effects are positively moderated by consumer AI literacy. Related Work: Existing work separates responsible AI into technical (privacy, fairness, robustness, explainability) and ethical/institutional (governance, social welfare, public well-being) concerns; CSR literature links corporate responsibility to consumer outcomes but typically treats responsibility as unidimensional or context-specific; prior measurement efforts are narrow, often tailored to a single sector or a small set of indicators and lack validated multidimensional scales for consumer perceptions of AI social responsibility. Empirical studies document that trust/credibility and perceived empathy or affect shape human–AI interactions, but they rarely decompose AI responsibility into technical versus institutional pathways or test parallel mediating mechanisms and moderators such as AI literacy. Limitations of prior approaches include single-dimension constructs, limited measurement validation, inadequate mediation/moderation testing, reliance on single-country convenience panels, and minimal cross-domain replication. Abstract: Problem: There is no validated consumer-centered measurement of AI social responsibility (AISR) that distinguishes technical safeguards from institutional ethics, nor an established causal model linking AISR dimensions to consumer brand advocacy. Approach: We present a structured research pipeline combining grounded qualitative scale development, large-scale psychometric validation, and preregistered randomized experiments to test causal pathways. Contributions: (1) an 18-item, two-dimensional AISR scale (technical: safety/usability/reflexivity; institutional: ethics/well-being) validated via EFA/CFA and reliability/validity metrics; (2) experimental tests of dual indirect pathways from AISR to brand advocacy—technical AISR → perceived AI credibility → advocacy; institutional AISR → perceived AI empathy → advocacy—and the moderating role of AI literacy; (3) cross-domain and cross-cultural replication plan. Expected outcome: A validated measurement instrument and a replicable causal model that clarifies how distinct AISR dimensions differentially drive consumer advocacy and how AI literacy conditions those effects. Experiments: Phase A — Scale validation (cross-sectional survey): Datasets: three online panels (China: Credamo, US/UK: Prolific, global sample: MTurk) combined for measurement invariance testing. Target N per country: 400 valid respondents (after exclusions) → total N=1200. Instruments: 18-item AISR candidate scale; perceived AI credibility (4 items); perceived AI empathy (3 items); brand advocacy (existing 3–5 items); AI literacy (4 items); social desirability control scale. Analyses: item-level descriptive statistics, EFA (principal axis factoring, oblique rotation) on half-sample, CFA on holdout half; fit indices: CFI>0.95, RMSEA<0.08, SRMR<0.08; reliability: Cronbach's alpha>0.7, composite reliability>0.7; convergent validity: AVE>0.5; discriminant validity: Fornell-Larcker. Measurement invariance: configural, metric, scalar across countries. Baselines: single-dimension AISR (collapsed), previously used responsible-AI proxies. Ablation: remove each subfactor and re-test fit and predictive validity. Phase B — Experiment 1 (mediated effects): Datasets: two-arm online randomized between-subjects experiment within each country. Manipulations: vignette+visual describing identical AI service with either technical AISR cues (privacy guarantees, explainability, safety features) or institutional AISR cues (ethics board, social programs, wellbeing initiatives). Sample: N=400 per country (200 per condition). Measures: post-manipulation AISR manipulation check; perceived AI credibility; perceived AI empathy; brand advocacy; control covariates (demographics, AI experience). Analyses: ANOVA on manipulation checks; mediation testing via SEM and bootstrap indirect effects (5000 samples); report effect sizes and 95% CIs. Baselines: no-AISR control condition (additional N=200 per country) and single-dimension AISR text. Phase C — Experiment 2 (moderated mediation): Design: 2 (AISR type: technical vs institutional) × continuous AI literacy moderator; random assignment with stratification by pre-measured AI literacy tertiles. Sample: N=1000 pooled (approx. 250 per cell across regions). Analyses: moderated mediation (PROCESS Model 8 or SEM equivalent) with bootstrap (5000); test interaction terms between AISR condition and AI literacy on mediators; test conditional indirect effects at -1SD, mean, +1SD of AI literacy. Ablations and robustness: domain replication within e-commerce, healthcare, and financial service vignettes (repeat Experiments 1–2 in each domain with N≥300 per domain), test alternative mediator sets (perceived justice, perceived competence), and run sensitivity analyses for common-method variance (Harman's single-factor, marker variable). Preregistration: all experimental materials, manipulation texts, and analysis scripts to be preregistered; significance threshold α=0.05; power analyses target 90% power to detect medium effects (f=0.25). Risk Factors and Limitations: Measurement risks: the 18-item AISR scale may not be invariant across cultures, languages, or domains; item interpretation may vary resulting in biased factor structure. Self-report and social desirability: ethics-related items and advocacy measures may be inflated. Manipulation risks: vignette-based manipulations may not generalize to real-world AI interactions and may differentially evoke unwanted emotional cues. Sampling biases: online panels overrepresent certain demographics and underrepresent elderly or low-technology-access populations, limiting generalizability. Common-method variance: cross-sectional survey and single-session experiments may induce inflated mediator–outcome correlations. Statistical risks: mediator constructs (credibility vs empathy) may be correlated, producing multicollinearity and ambiguous causal ordering. Power and effect-size sensitivity: small effects in some domains may require larger samples than planned. Domain and regulatory heterogeneity: results obtained in e-commerce may not transfer to high-stakes domains (healthcare, finance) where technical risks dominate. Ethical and legal constraints: cross-border data collection must comply with local privacy laws; some AISR manipulations (e.g., claims of audits) could raise deception/ethics review issues. Computational limits: SEM with large multi-group models and invariance testing may require substantial compute and careful model trimming to avoid convergence failures.
